question.:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{3-4x}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=3-4x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3-4x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-4x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-4x|+C & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-4x|-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-4x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|3-4x|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{1}{3-4x}\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|3-4x|).
$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{6-x}\,\text{d}x.$ Assume that $K$ is an arbitrary positive constant.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let $u=6-x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=-\text{d}u.
$$

We can now rewrite the integral in terms of $u,$ solve it, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{6-x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot (-1)\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|6-x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the above by writing $C=-\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ for another arbitrary constant $K,$ and then we can combine the two terms using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|6-x|+C & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|6-x|-\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡|6-x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|6-x|)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we finally conclude that

$$
\int \frac{1}{6-x}\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|6-x|).
$$
